facts.statement: Strigogyps fossils date from the Middle Eocene to the Early Oligocene periods.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Eocene to Early Oligocene

facts.statement: Strigogyps lived in France and Germany during the Middle Eocene and Early Oligocene.
facts.quote: Strigogyps is an extinct genus of prehistoric bird from the Middle Eocene to Early Oligocene of France and Germany.

facts.statement: Strigogyps was approximately the size of a large chicken or guan, weighing less than 1 kilogram.
facts.quote: It was probably around the size of a large chicken or a guan, weighing not quite 1 kg.

facts.statement: The species Strigogyps sapea was likely flightless based on the ratio of its wing to leg bone lengths.
facts.quote: Apparently, as indicated by the ratio of lengths of wing to leg bones, S. sapea was flightless.

facts.statement: Strigogyps had legs not adapted for running, suggesting a walking lifestyle similar to that of trumpeters.
facts.quote: Its legs were not adapted to running, so it seems to have had a walking lifestyle similar to trumpeters.

facts.statement: While other Cariamiformes were mostly carnivorous, Strigogyps sapea likely had a facultatively herbivorous or omnivorous diet.
facts.quote: Unlike other Cariamiformes which appear to have been mostly carnivorous, the specimens of one species, Strigogyps sapea, suggest a facultatively herbivorous or omnivorous diet.

facts.statement: The type species Strigogyps dubius was described by Gaillard in 1908.
facts.quote: The type species of Strigogyps is S. dubius, which was described by Gaillard in 1908.

facts.statement: Strigogyps was initially classified in the owl order Strigiformes and considered a sophiornithid.
facts.quote: It was initially placed in the owl order Strigiformes and considered to be a sophiornithid.

facts.statement: The species S. dubius is based on a single tibiotarsus found in the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene Quercy phosphorites of France.
facts.quote: S. dubius is based on a single tibiotarsus from the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene Quercy phosphorites of France.

facts.statement: The original tibiotarsus of S. dubius was destroyed during the bombing of Munich in World War II, though casts remain.
facts.quote: This tibiotarsus was destroyed in World War II during the bombing of Munich, but casts remain.

facts.statement: Lambrecht described Eocathartes robustus and Geiseloceros robustus in 1935 from the Middle Eocene Geisel Valley of Germany.
facts.quote: In 1935, Lambrecht described a new New World vulture, Eocathartes robustus, and a hornbill, Geiseloceros robustus, from the Middle Eocene (Lutetian) of the Geisel Valley of Germany.

facts.statement: Mayr (2007) determined that Eocathartes robustus and Geiseloceros robustus are synonymous and represent the species Strigogyps robustus.
facts.quote: Mayr (2007) found them to be synonymous and a species of Strigogyps, S. robustus.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest Strigogyps is a basal member of Cariamae and not closely related to phorusrhachids.
facts.quote: Recent studies (Alvarenga and Höfling 2003, Mayr 2005) have found Strigogyps to be a more basal member of Cariamae, and not particularly close to the phorusrhachids.

facts.statement: Salmila robusta is considered more basal than Strigogyps, with the clade of Salmila and Cariamae being the sister taxon to Psophiidae within Gruiformes.
facts.quote: Salmila robusta, another bird from Messel was found to be more basal than Strigogyps, and the clade composed of Salmila and Cariamae to be the sister taxon to Psophiidae within a monophyletic Gruiformes.

facts.statement: Strigogyps belongs to the order Cariamiformes.
facts.quote: ordo: Cariamiformes

facts.statement: Strigogyps is classified within the family Ameghinornithidae.
facts.quote: familia: Ameghinornithidae

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database lists Strigidae as the parent group for Strigogyps.
facts.quote: Parent group: Strigidae

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database classifies Strigogyps within the family Strigidae.
facts.quote: Family: Strigidae

facts.statement: Strigogyps lived between 48.07 and 33.9 million years ago, from the Lutetian to the Priabonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Lutetian to Priabonian (48.07 to 33.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is debated whether fragmentary remains from the Palaeocene and Eocene of England and North America are phorusrhachids, though they are likely not.
facts.quote: Fragmentary remains from the Palaeocene and/or Eocene of England and North America have also been suggested to be phorusrhachids, but, like Strigogyps, they probably are not.
